name: Parthian Empire (Orodes II)

areaKm2.note: Seshat codes 2,000,000 km2 for 100 BCE and 3,000,000 km2 for 1 CE; mid interpolated. The historical-basemaps world_bc100 "Parthia" polygon covers only Parthia proper (473,839 km2 computed on the sphere) and leaves Mesopotamia and Media inside its "Seleucid Kingdom" polygon, so it is not used for the area.

population.note: Seshat codes Parthian Empire I at 5,450,000 for 100 BCE (low) and gives three disputed values for 1 CE: 7,500,000, 15,000,000 and 25,000,000. Mid ~8 million for 53 BCE, after the conquest of Mesopotamia and Media but before later growth; the 25 million figure is treated as an outlier. Everything inside the realm including the vassal kingdoms (Characene, Elymais, Persis, Adiabene, Osroene); Armenia, at war with Parthia in 53, is not counted.

urbanization.note: Educated guess. Seshat (https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/125) codes the largest settlement at 300,000 for 100 BCE (Seleucia on the Tigris). Mesopotamia was highly urban (Seleucia, Ctesiphon, Babylon), the Iranian plateau and Parthia proper much less.

activePersonnel.note: Educated guess. No standing army; this is the force under arms in the 53 BCE campaign season: Surena's ~10,000 horsemen (Wiesehofer, Ancient Persia from 550 BC to 650 AD (2001), pp. 137-138, 147-148 and n. on p. 279-280 (https://archive.org/details/AncientPersiaFrom550BcTo650Ad2001)), the royal army in Armenia, eastern frontier forces and city garrisons (see forces) + the camel and baggage train (supportPersonnel). Mid = P roles 50,000 + support 4,000, rounded. Convention: noble retinues already called up for the 53 BCE campaign are counted as active (wartime snapshot at campaign start); retinues not called up are in trainedReserves.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess. Noble retinues not called up in 53; Justin (41.2, quoted by Wiesehofer p. 137, https://archive.org/details/AncientPersiaFrom550BcTo650Ad2001) gives 50,000 horsemen against Antony in 36 BCE (ancient figure), which bounds what the nobility could field within a season.

supportPersonnel.note: Educated guess. Camel drivers, grooms and baggage servants: Surena alone travelled with 1,000 baggage camels (Plutarch Crassus 21, https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Plutarch/Lives/Crassus*.html) and the camels carrying spare arrows at Carrhae (Crassus 25) needed handlers.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess. No standing army: the king called up the nobles, who brought retinues of dependants (Wiesehofer, Ancient Persia from 550 BC to 650 AD (2001), pp. 137-138, 147-148 and n. on p. 279-280 (https://archive.org/details/AncientPersiaFrom550BcTo650Ad2001): "The richer someone is, the more horsemen he provides for the king", Justin 41.2). Justin's 50,000 horsemen against Antony in 36 BCE (ancient figure) would be ~0.6% of an 8 million population; 0.025 allows for a fuller call-up including foot levies.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Surena's 1,000 cataphracts at Carrhae (Plutarch Crassus 21, https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Plutarch/Lives/Crassus*.html; accepted by Koselenko, Wolski and von Gall as summarised by Wiesehofer, Ancient Persia from 550 BC to 650 AD (2001), pp. 137-138, 147-148 and n. on p. 279-280 (https://archive.org/details/AncientPersiaFrom550BcTo650Ad2001)) + the cataphracts of the royal army that Orodes II led into Armenia and of other noble retinues (unknown; 1,000-7,000 estimated).

quality.note: Rubric 1.0: fully armoured men and horses with the kontos, "Margianian steel" (Plutarch, quoted by Wiesehofer p. 148), the era's best heavy cavalry.

training.note: Noble warriors trained from childhood (rubric 0.75); no unit drill on the Roman pattern.

count.note: Surena's horse archers: ~9,000 (Wolski) to 10,000 (von Gall) per Wiesehofer, Ancient Persia from 550 BC to 650 AD (2001), pp. 137-138, 147-148 and n. on p. 279-280 (https://archive.org/details/AncientPersiaFrom550BcTo650Ad2001), from Plutarch's "no fewer than ten thousand" horsemen, vassals and slaves (Crassus 21, https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Plutarch/Lives/Crassus*.html) + mounted archers of the royal army in Armenia (Plutarch: Orodes attacked Armenia "with an overwhelming force", Crassus 22; size unknown, 5,000-30,000 estimated) + eastern frontier and satrapal horse (1,000-10,000 estimated).

quality.note: Rubric 0.75-1.0: powerful composite bows and an arrow resupply by camel train at Carrhae (Plutarch Crassus 25), which made the horse archers decisive.

training.note: Dependants trained in riding and archery from childhood (Justin 41.2, quoted by Wiesehofer p. 137); not drilled as units.

count.note: Educated guess. Foot levies with javelins and spears of the royal army and vassal kings; Wiesehofer (https://archive.org/details/AncientPersiaFrom550BcTo650Ad2001, p. 148) calls infantry "of secondary importance" and cites only the Chronicle of Arbela's 20,000 foot against the Alans in 136 CE.
Educated guess. Foot archers and slingers of the levies and of the hill peoples (Elymaeans, Mardians); no figure survives.
Educated guess. Garrisons and militias of the Greek cities (Seleucia, Babylon, Susa) and mercenaries of the king; close-order infantry played almost no role in Parthian field armies.

commandQuality.note: Rubric 0.75 for Surena (proven commander: the camel arrow resupply and combined cataphract/horse-archer tactics at Carrhae) but no staff system and royal distrust (Orodes executed Surena soon after); mid 0.7.

cohesion.note: Rubric 0.25-0.5: feudal host of noble retinues (Wiesehofer p. 137: pelatai and douloi of the aristocracy); retainers loyal to their lord rather than the king, dynastic strife frequent.

morale.note: Rubric 0.75: defending Mesopotamia against invasion, confident in cavalry superiority over Roman infantry in open country.

weapons.note: Anchor 3 (iron weapons) with powerful composite bows and the kontos; no torsion artillery in field use.

armor.note: Anchor 3 (mail) plus full horse armour of the cataphracts, anticipating anchor 4 barding; horse archers unarmoured.

ships.note: No navy. Anchor 1-2: river craft on the Tigris and Euphrates; Gulf shipping belonged to the vassal kingdom of Characene.

fortification.note: Anchor 2-3: mudbrick and Hellenistic city walls (Seleucia, Nisa); the Parthians rarely conducted or resisted formal sieges.

logistics.note: Anchor 2-3: camel and pack-horse trains (Surena's 1,000 camels), living off grazing; the Achaemenid depot system was not maintained.

communications.note: Anchor 3 (mounted relay posts): royal roads with stations (stathmoi) listed by Isidore of Charax.

isr.note: Year anchor 3: mounted scouts and guides (the Arab chief Ariamnes misled Crassus, Plutarch Crassus 21).

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project Database 2023 via https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-maddison-project-database.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true: year 1 CE values for Iran and Iraq are 1,116 (2011 int$), Turkey 897. Applied to Parthian Mesopotamia and Iran with a slightly lower mid for the pastoral north-east.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. Military service was owed by the nobility and their dependants in return for land, so little of the military burden passed through a royal treasury; share of output devoted to horses, arms and retinues estimated.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess. Agrarian and pastoral economy; crafts and caravan trade (Silk Road via Merv and Seleucia).

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. Irrigated Mesopotamian agriculture produced large surpluses; the plateau and the north-east much less.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in an ancient Greek-type age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model used for all classical and medieval snapshots.

roadKm.note: Educated guess. Royal roads inherited from the Achaemenids and Seleucids: the Zeugma-Seleucia-Ecbatana-Merv-Arachosia route described by Isidore of Charax ran several thousand km; no engineered network on the Roman pattern.

majorPorts.note: Educated guess. Charax Spasinou and the river ports of Seleucia/Ctesiphon; no war fleet to supply.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess. Gulf and river shipping of the Characene and Mesopotamian merchants; no source gives a tonnage.

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess. Cavalry armies living off grazing with camel trains could operate further from depots than infantry (Engels, isbn:0520042727, ch. 1 for the infantry baseline of 1-2 weeks); desert stretches limited them.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. ~0.08-0.2 horses, camels, mules and donkeys per inhabitant x population (horse-breeding aristocracy, Nisaean horses of Media, camels of Mesopotamia).

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.3 elements: deep strategic depth and a hot, dry climate the Roman infantry was not adapted to (Plutarch Crassus 22 on the waterless desert march), plus local supply and population support; few fortified cities, hence mid 1.25.

notes: Snapshot = spring-summer 53 BCE, Crassus' invasion: Orodes II split his forces, invading Armenia himself while Surena met Crassus at Carrhae with ~10,000 horse. Border: historical-basemaps world_bc100 (latest file at or before -53) has only Parthia proper as "Parthia" (473,839 km2) and still shows Mesopotamia and Media as "Seleucid Kingdom"; world_bc1 ("Parthian Empire", ~1.93 million km2) is closer to the real 53 BCE extent but post-dates it. areaKm2 is researched (Seshat). All force numbers are reconstructions: Plutarch's figures for Surena are accepted by modern scholars (Wolski, Koselenko, von Gall as summarised by Wiesehofer), but nothing is known about the size of the royal army in Armenia or the eastern forces, so the total active strength is an educated guess. Sheldon (Rome's Wars in Parthia, 2010) and Overtoom (Reign of Arrows, 2020) were not fetched. Population convention: inside the real 53 BCE realm incl. vassal kingdoms; Armenia excluded.
